facts.text: A founder letter is the annual public document a CEO or co-founder writes directly to owners - shareholders, users, or the general "fellow travelers" audience - to account for the year, reaffirm operating principles, admit mistakes, and frame what comes next. It is the genre Warren Buffett perfected at Berkshire Hathaway (1977–present), Jeff Bezos institutionalized at Amazon (1997–2020), and Patrick and John Collison adopted at Stripe (2019–present).
The form is distinct from:
An internal executive memo (which talks down the org chart, not out to owners)
A press release or marketing post (which is selling, not reporting)
An op-ed (which argues a public-interest point, not company-specific accountability)
A whitepaper (which makes a technical or policy case, not a stewardship report)

What makes a founder letter work is candor, operating principles that repeat year over year, and a long-horizon frame ("Day 1," "10-year zoom-out") that lets the reader weigh the current year against the company's deeper trajectory.
Write as if to an intelligent non-specialist who owns shares and deserves the truth in plain English. Pronoun is "we" or "your company," never "the corporation."
Three beats: (1) Where we are - year's results in plain terms. (2) What we learned - what went wrong, what surprised us. (3) Where we're going - unchanging principles plus bets for next 5–10 years.
Bezos re-attached the 1997 letter to every subsequent letter for 20 years. Buffett restates Berkshire's "owner-related business principles" nearly every letter. Repetition is a feature.
Name a specific mistake. Explain why you made it. Say what you changed. Vague self-criticism ("we have work to do") does not count.
Amazon's "It's still Day 1." Buffett's 10- and 20-year per-share book value comparison. Pick a frame, stick to it, refer to it in every letter.
Bezos's 2007 frame: missionaries paradoxically make more money than mercenaries trying to flip stock.
Treat capital allocation as the most important decision the CEO makes that year.
Pick 3–5 metrics that genuinely run the business and report them every year. Amazon: free cash flow per share. Stripe: total volume processed. Berkshire: operating earnings and per-share book value.

facets.title: 9. Voice: short sentences, plain words, dry humor

facts.text: Buffett uses short transitions and conversational rhythm. Avoid corporate passive voice and AI-isms.
End with a signature and a date. Two co-founders sign together if the company is co-founded.
PR-spin letter (every metric reframed as a win)
Earnings-call regurgitation
Mission-statement-as-letter
First-year-only candor
Ghostwritten throughout
No signature, no date
AI-flavored prose ("leverage," "robust," "comprehensive")
Hiding the mistake in a footnote
Founder letter vs executive memo? Founder letter if audience is owners/public and cadence is annual.
How long? 1,500 words minimum. 4,000 ceiling. Bezos averaged ~2,500.
First-person singular or plural? Singular ("I") for honesty section. Plural ("we") for company actions.
Include forward guidance? Specific numbers build credibility if you're willing to be held to them.
First-ever founder letter (year 1)? Spine compresses. Aim 1,500–2,000 words. The 1997 Bezos letter is canonical.
Public vs private company? Public letters carry SEC-adjacent obligations.
